svg.title: Networking timeline: production-relevant milestones
svg.desc: A timeline from 1969 to 2022. 1969: ARPANET first message (UCLA → SRI). Packet switching becomes the model. 1973: Ethernet invented at Xerox PARC (Metcalfe). 1974: Cerf and Kahn: gateways connecting separate networks. The internetworking design every packet still follows. 1980: DIX Ethernet II specification; IEEE 802.3 follows (1983). Maximum payload of 1500 bytes. RFC 894 (1984) carries IP over it: the 1500-byte IP MTU you will meet for your entire career. 1981: IPv4 (RFC 791) and TCP (RFC 793) specified. 32-bit addresses: about 4.3 billion. Seemed enormous. Was not. 1983: ARPANET’s NCP-to-TCP/IP transition deadline (1 January). 1983: First DNS specifications (RFC 882/883); base specs RFC 1034/1035 in 1987. Replaces one shared hosts.txt file The hosts file still exists on your machine and still overrides DNS. 1986: Congestion collapse: throughput between LBL and UC Berkeley drops from 32 kbit/s to 40 bit/s. 1988: Jacobson’s congestion avoidance and control added to TCP. Slow start, congestion window, retransmit backoff — why TCP slows down when it sees loss (Modules 11, 14). 1988: Morris worm (sendmail, fingerd, rsh trust, weak passwords). Security was not in the original design; CERT/CC is founded. 1989: BGP (RFC 1105); BGP-4 in 1994, current spec RFC 4271 (2006). Policy routing between independent networks. 1991: The World Wide Web goes public (Berners-Lee, CERN). HTTP on top of TCP; networking becomes mainstream infrastructure. 1993: CIDR (RFC 1518/1519) replaces class-based addressing. Buys IPv4 decades and makes route aggregation possible. 1994: NAT described (RFC 1631). Many hosts share one public IP. Breaks end-to-end reachability; NAT state is behind many idle-timeout and port-exhaustion incidents. 1995: NSFNET backbone retired; the commercial internet takes over. 1995: First IPv6 specification (RFC 1883); current spec RFC 8200 (2017). 128-bit addresses — and three decades of partial adoption. 1995: SSL 2.0 (Netscape); SSL 3.0 in 1996. 1999: TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246). 2006: Amazon EC2 launches. Networks become API objects: VPCs, security groups, route tables. 2008: Kaminsky DNS cache-poisoning attack. Resolvers randomise source ports as well as query IDs (you will watch this in the lab). 2011: IANA allocates its last free IPv4 blocks to the regional registries. IPv4 becomes something you buy; CGNAT and paid cloud public IPs follow. 2013: Docker; 2014 — Kubernetes. Network namespaces, veth pairs, and overlays become everyday tools. 2015: HTTP/2 (RFC 7540; now RFC 9113). Fixes HTTP head-of-line blocking, not TCP head-of-line blocking. 2015: Let’s Encrypt opens to the public. Free automated certificates; HTTPS becomes the default. 2016: Mirai botnet floods Dyn’s DNS service. Many large sites unreachable for hours because their DNS provider was. 2018: TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446). 1-RTT handshake, encrypted certificate, forward secrecy required. 2021: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 formally deprecated (RFC 8996). 2021: Facebook withdraws its own BGP routes. Its DNS servers become unreachable, so its names stop resolving worldwide — and its internal tools fail with them. 2021: QUIC (RFC 9000); 2022 — HTTP/3 (RFC 9114). Transport over UDP, encrypted by design; no TCP head-of-line blocking. 2022: TCP consolidated in RFC 9293. Folds in decades of updates; wire format and handshake unchanged.
